written.q: Explain the difference between crisp and fuzzy sets and logic, with examples, and state two advantages of fuzzy control.
written.a: A crisp set: membership is 0 or 1 ('the car is red'; hot = temperature at least 30 °C, so 29.9 and 30 are totally different). A fuzzy set: partial membership in [0, 1] (distance to the car ahead is partly 'close' and partly 'far'; μB = 1/x1 + … + 0.7/x4 + 0.3/x5 for 'young'). Boolean logic answers yes/no; fuzzy logic gives degrees (0.9, 0.25, 0.1). Advantages: no accurate quantitative model is required, deals with vague systems using linguistic variables, closer to human thinking, faster and simpler controller development (Sendai subway: 10 % less energy, smooth ride).

written.q: Define fuzzy set, fuzzy variable, linguistic variable, linguistic hedge and fuzzy proposition.
written.a: Fuzzy set: each element y has a membership μX(y) in [0, 1]. Fuzzy variable: a variable whose values are fuzzy sets. Linguistic variable: a fuzzy variable with word values (freezing, cool, warm, hot). Linguistic hedge: a modifier such as very or somewhat (very A = μ²). Fuzzy proposition: a sentence like 'Joe is short' whose truth value is the membership μshort(Joe), 0 meaning absolute falsity and 1 absolute truth.

written.q: Give the fuzzy union, intersection and complement formulas and compute them for μ<sub>A</sub> = 0.3 and μ<sub>B</sub> = 0.9.
written.a: Union max(μA, μB) = 0.9; intersection min = 0.3; complement of A = 1 − 0.3 = 0.7.

written.q: Describe the components of a fuzzy system and the role of each, using the air-conditioner example.
written.a: Crisp input (room temperature, target) → fuzzifier (membership functions turn it into degrees such as cold, warm, hot) → inference (applies the fuzzy rules built from the fuzzy sets, e.g. IF temperature is hot AND target is warm THEN command is cool, taken from the expert-written associative matrix) → defuzzifier (turns the fuzzy conclusion into one value) → crisp output (heat, cool or no change, or a speed).

written.q: Write the triangular and trapezoidal membership functions and compute triangle (20, 25, 30) at 23 and trapezoid (20, 25, 30, 35) at 22, 28 and 33.
written.a: Triangular (a, m, b): 0 for x ≤ a or x ≥ b; (x − a)/(m − a) for a < x ≤ m; (b − x)/(b − m) for m < x < b. Trapezoidal (a, b, c, d): (x − a)/(b − a) on a to b; 1 on b to c; (d − x)/(d − c) on c to d; else 0. Triangle at 23: 3/5 = 0.6. Trapezoid at 22: 2/5 = 0.4; at 28: 1; at 33: 2/5 = 0.4.

written.q: Explain Mamdani inference step by step (antecedent, implication, aggregation), using service = 3 and food = 8 for 'service is excellent OR food is delicious'.
written.a: 1) Fuzzify inputs and evaluate the antecedent: excellent(3) = 0.0, delicious(8) = 0.7; OR = max = 0.7 (the rule strength). 2) Implication: use the minimum to truncate the consequent (tip is generous) at 0.7 (the product would scale it instead). 3) Aggregation: combine the clipped curves of all rules with max (or sum, probabilistic sum) into one fuzzy output; then defuzzify (centroid), giving e.g. tip = 16.7 %.

written.q: Defuzzify a combined output with degrees 0.4 at speeds 40, 50, 60 and 0.6 at speeds 70, 80, 90, 100 using the centroid. Compare with Sugeno constants 50 and 80 at strengths 0.4 and 0.6.
written.a: Top = 40×0.4 + 50×0.4 + 60×0.4 + 70×0.6 + 80×0.6 + 90×0.6 + 100×0.6 = 264; bottom = 3×0.4 + 4×0.6 = 3.6; output 73.3. Sugeno: (0.4×50 + 0.6×80)/(0.4 + 0.6) = 68. Mamdani needs the output curves; Sugeno only needs constants.

written.q: For the heater controller at 35 °F and 1 °F/hr, four rules fire with strengths 0.6 (FAST), 0.4 (SLOW), 0.4 (FAST) and 0.8 (MEDIUM). Find the crisp motor speed given peaks FAST 800, MEDIUM 500, SLOW 300.
written.a: y = (0.6×800 + 0.4×300 + 0.4×800 + 0.8×500)/(0.6 + 0.4 + 0.4 + 0.8) = (480 + 120 + 320 + 400)/2.2 = 1320/2.2 = 600 R/M. Rule strengths are the minimum of the temperature and change-rate degrees.
